idiom_name: class with #private state whose mutations run through a serialised (queued) path
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the one thing the classic structure cares about that JavaScript lacks: real encapsulation at compile time - `#private` (or `private`) fields make the guarded state unreachable from outside the class, so the guardian's monopoly is checked by the compiler rather than by a convention. The runtime is still single-threaded JavaScript, so what plays the lock's role is a single-owner serialisation discipline: the state stays in the class, every mutation is expressed as a task on a promise chain (or funnelled through a reducer whose only writer is the class), and no accessor hands out a live reference to the internal collection. For genuine parallelism in worker threads the shared state must be a `SharedArrayBuffer` touched through `Atomics`, or owned by one worker and reached by messages; TypeScript's types cannot express either of those guarantees, only document them.
pitfalls: `private` is erased at runtime and `(obj as any).field` defeats it; only `#`-fields (or a closure) actually keep the state out of reach.
Returning the internal array - or typing it `readonly Entry[]`, which is also erased - gives callers a live view of the guarded state; return a copy.
The type system cannot see interleaving: nothing stops a caller from awaiting between two calls that were meant to be one atomic transaction, so compound operations belong inside one queued task.
